title: Problems involving congruence and similarity
summary: Model maps, plans, photographs, shadows and indirect measurements using congruence or similarity.
objectives: Translate a real context into a scale or proportion.
Convert units before using a map or model scale.
Check whether length or area is being scaled.

blocks.text: Identify which measurements correspond, convert them to compatible units, and write a proportion. For shadows and indirect measurement, equal angles create similar triangles.

Scale drawings, maps and models are applications of similarity. A scale 1:n means one unit on the representation corresponds to n of the same units in reality. Convert units before multiplying or dividing by the scale factor.

Decide the direction: actual length=plan length×n, while plan length=actual length÷n. Areas use n². In nested scale problems, multiply successive linear factors first, then square only if the requested quantity is an area.

sections.title: Worked example

prompt.text: A 2 m pole casts a 3 m shadow while a tree casts a 12 m shadow. Find the tree height.

sections.verification_note: Check that every side and angle was matched in the stated corresponding order.

sections.title: Worked example: apply the method

prompt.text: A rectangular garden measures 36 m by 24 m. It is drawn at scale 1:600. Find the plan dimensions in centimetres and its plan area.

content.text: Convert actual lengths: 36 m=3600 cm and 24 m=2400 cm.
Divide by 600 to obtain plan dimensions 6 cm by 4 cm.

sections.verification_note: Using the area factor 600² gives 864 m²=8,640,000 cm² and 8,640,000÷360,000=24 cm².

blocks.text: Do not use metres on one side of a ratio and centimetres on the other. A 1:600 scale is a linear ratio; area changes by 600². Label whether each quantity belongs to the plan, model or real object.

prompt.text: A 1:100 plan shows a wall as 6 cm. Find the real wall length in metres.

feedback.text: The real length is 600 cm, which is 6 m.

blocks.text: Write the correspondence first, use one consistent scale factor, preserve equal angles, and check whether a length, perimeter or area needs a linear or squared factor.
Before moving on, explain the relevant property in words, show the equation or formula with units, and use the diagram markings to check that every correspondence is consistent.
